theory.intro: Faults in sampling, survey questions and comparisons can make conclusions unreliable. Check who is included, who is missing, whether questions and response choices are clear, and whether a comparison group is needed.
facts: A biased, or unrepresentative, sample does not accurately represent the population.
**Selection bias** occurs when the selected group misrepresents the population. Random selection within an unsuitable group does not fix this.
A **small sample** may miss the variety in the population.
**Volunteer bias** can occur when people choose whether to participate. People who reply may differ from those who do not.
**Survivorship bias** occurs when only successful or surviving cases are considered and failures are left out.
A **leading question** encourages a preferred answer through emotional language or one-sided information.
**Ambiguous questions** and vague response choices can be interpreted differently. State a clear time frame when needed and provide suitable choices without overlapping boundaries.
A comparable **control group** without the tested programme helps show whether an improvement would occur anyway. Keep other relevant conditions the same.

workedExamples.question_text:
A council wants to know residents' opinions about a new park.
(a) It interviews only members of a local gardening club. Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
(b) It instead invites all residents to reply online, but only $36$ of $600$ residents reply. Explain why the replies alone may not represent all residents.
(c) It interviews only $3$ residents. Explain the problem with this sample.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Gardening club members may have different views about parks from other residents. The sample leaves out the views of residents outside the club.
(b) Residents who choose to reply may have different views from those who do not. Inviting everyone does not make the replies representative of everyone.
(c) Three residents may not cover the variety of opinions in the population.

workedExamples.question_text:
A student plans a survey about a new school library.
(a) Explain a fault in: 'Do you agree that our wonderful new library is excellent?'
(b) The only response choices are 'Excellent', 'Good' and 'Satisfactory'. Explain a fault in these choices.
(c) Suggest more suitable wording and a response section.
(d) Explain a fault in: 'Do you visit the library and borrow books?'
(e) Write a suitable question to find out how long students spend reading.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) 'Wonderful' and 'excellent' present the library positively and encourage a favourable answer. This is a leading question.
(b) There is no choice for a negative opinion. Students who are dissatisfied cannot give a suitable answer.
(c) Ask: 'How would you rate the new school library?'
Provide: Very good, Good, Neither good nor poor, Poor, Very poor, Have not used it.
(d) Visiting and borrowing are different actions. A student might visit without borrowing, so one answer cannot clearly describe both.
(e) Ask: 'How many hours did you spend reading outside lessons during the past seven days?' Allow a numerical answer, including zero.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) A school introduces a revision programme. The mean test mark increases from $11$ before the programme to $14$ afterwards. What other information would help show whether the programme caused the improvement?
(b) A study of delivery businesses includes only businesses still operating after five years. Explain why this may give a misleading picture of business success.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Compare the improvement with a comparable control group that did not use the programme. Use comparable tests over the same period and keep other relevant conditions the same. Marks might improve without the programme.
(b) Businesses that closed are excluded. Looking only at surviving businesses leaves out failures and can make success appear more common. This is survivorship bias.

workedExamples.question_text: A survey asks: 'How often do you buy lunch?' The choices are 'Rarely', 'Sometimes' and 'Often'. Another question asks how long lunch takes, with choices '$0$–$10$ minutes', '$10$–$20$ minutes' and '$20$–$30$ minutes'. Explain the faults in the questions and response choices.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The first question gives no time frame. Respondents may answer about different periods.
'Rarely', 'Sometimes' and 'Often' may mean different frequencies to different people.
The time intervals overlap at $10$ and $20$ minutes, so those answers fit two choices.
There is no choice for a lunch taking more than $30$ minutes.

foundation.question_text:
A school wants to find out students' favourite subjects. It surveys only students in an optional mathematics club.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text: Mathematics club members may be more interested in mathematics than other students. Their favourite subjects may not represent those of all students.

foundation.question_text:
A school runs a new reading programme. The mean test mark rises from $12$ before the programme to $15$ afterwards.
What other information would help show whether the programme caused the improvement?
foundation.solution_text:
Compare the improvement with a comparable control group that did not use the programme.
Use comparable tests over the same period and keep other relevant conditions the same. Marks might improve without the programme.

foundation.question_text:
A survey asks: 'How often do you exercise?' Its response choices are 'A little' and 'A lot'.
Explain why the question and choices may give unreliable results.
foundation.solution_text:
The question does not specify a time frame, so respondents may answer about different periods.
'A little' and 'A lot' are vague and may mean different amounts to different people.

foundation.question_text:
A council wants to know residents' opinions about a new footpath. It asks only $2$ residents from a town of $800$ people.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text: Two residents may not cover the variety of opinions among the town's residents. Their views alone may not represent the population.

foundation.question_text:
A survey asks: 'Don't you agree that the new school timetable is brilliant?'
Suggest more suitable wording and a response section.
foundation.solution_text:
Ask: 'What is your opinion of the new school timetable?'
Provide: Very favourable, Favourable, Neither favourable nor unfavourable, Unfavourable, Very unfavourable, Not sure.
This removes the praise and allows both positive and negative opinions.

foundation.question_text:
A survey about a swimming pool asks: 'How would you rate the pool?' The only choices are 'Excellent', 'Good' and 'Satisfactory'.
Explain why the response section may give biased results.
foundation.solution_text: The choices provide no way to report a poor experience. Respondents with negative opinions cannot choose an answer that represents their view.

foundation.question_text:
A hospital surveys discharged patients by mailing $1000$ questionnaires.
Only $80$ patients reply, and the hospital records their responses without following up the remaining $920$ patients.
Identify the data collection fault.
foundation.solution_text:
$80$ of $1000$ replied, so $920$ did not: $\frac{920}{1000}\times100\%=92\%$.
The patients who replied may have different experiences from those who did not. Without follow-up, their answers alone may not represent all discharged patients.
High non-response and a risk of non-response bias.

development.question_text:
A study asks people at a railway station how residents of the whole town travel to work.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
development.solution_text: People at the station are more likely to use trains than other residents. The sample may miss people who drive, walk, cycle or work from home, so it may overstate train use.

development.question_text:
A school introduces a homework programme. Its mean test mark increases from $18$ to $22$.
What other information would help show whether the programme caused the increase?
development.solution_text:
Find out how marks changed for a comparable control group that did not use the programme.
Use comparable tests over the same period and keep other relevant conditions the same. The comparison helps show whether improvement would occur without the programme.

development.question_text:
A survey asks how much time students spent online yesterday. Its only choices are '$0$–$2$ hours', '$2$–$4$ hours' and '$4$–$6$ hours'.
Explain two faults in the response section.
development.solution_text:
The boundaries overlap: exactly $2$ hours fits the first two choices, and exactly $4$ hours fits the last two.
There is no choice for more than $6$ hours online.

development.question_text:
A study investigates how successful new restaurants are. It includes only restaurants that are still open after four years.
Explain why the conclusion may be misleading, with reference to survivorship bias.
development.solution_text: Restaurants that closed during the four years are excluded. The sample contains only survivors and leaves out failures, so it may make restaurant success appear more common than it is.

development.question_text:
A survey asks: 'Considering that the new sports centre will be very expensive, should the council build it?'
Explain why the question may give biased results.
development.solution_text: The question highlights the cost without giving information about possible benefits. This one-sided information may encourage respondents to oppose the sports centre.

development.question_text:
A student wants to find out how long classmates spend playing computer games.
Write a suitable survey question.
development.solution_text:
Ask: 'How many hours did you spend playing computer games during the past seven days?'
Allow a numerical answer, including zero. The activity and time frame are clear.

development.question_text:
A traffic department studies speeding on a local road by counting only the vehicles stopped by police patrol cars, while vehicles that passed without incident are unrecorded.
Identify the fault in this observational record.
development.solution_text:
Selection bias: selecting only vehicles stopped by police creates an unrepresentative sample of traffic on the road.
Vehicles that pass without being stopped are excluded, so the sample cannot show the speeding behaviour of all traffic. Do not assume every stopped driver was speeding.

mastery.question_text:
A supermarket wants to compare its value for money with another supermarket. Staff randomly stop shoppers at its own entrance and ask: 'Do you agree that our supermarket offers much better value?' The choices are 'Strongly agree', 'Agree' and 'Not sure'.
Give one criticism of the question, one of the response section and one of the sampling method.
mastery.solution_text:
The question presents the supermarket as better value and encourages agreement, so it is leading.
The response section has no disagreement choices, so shoppers cannot express an unfavourable comparison.
Shoppers at this supermarket may already prefer it. Randomly choosing among them does not represent shoppers across both supermarkets.

mastery.question_text:
A student wants to find out how classmates use an online revision site. The planned questions are: 'Do you have internet access at home and use the revision site?' and 'Don't you agree that the revision site is excellent?'
Give one criticism of each question. Then rewrite the second question with a suitable response section.
mastery.solution_text:
The first question asks about two different things. A student may have internet access but not use the site, so a single answer is unclear.
The second question encourages a positive answer through 'Don't you agree' and 'excellent'.
Ask: 'How would you rate the online revision site?'
Provide: Very good, Good, Neither good nor poor, Poor, Very poor, Have not used it.

mastery.question_text:
A sports club invites all members to complete a survey about whether they enjoy completing surveys. Of $400$ replies, $396$ say yes. The club concludes that nearly all members enjoy completing surveys.
Explain why this conclusion is not valid.
mastery.solution_text:
$\frac{396}{400}\times100\%=99\%$ of respondents said yes.
Members who enjoy completing surveys may be more likely to reply. Members who dislike them may not reply and are missing from the results.
The percentage describes the respondents; it does not establish that nearly all members enjoy completing surveys.
